world.name: The Village of Lost Hours
world.aesthetic_seed: a small clockmaker's village at the bottom of a dream, at dusk; warm lantern-light on brass and old oak, moss in the seams of stone, paper lanterns, soft watercolor edges, the gentle mystery of lost hours drifting down like leaves

exemplars.title: The Stair of Small Clocks
exemplars.seed: a narrow wooden stair where a small clock sits on every step, each ticking to its own slow count under a round window of dusk
exemplars.description: A small clock waits on every step, and no two agree on the time. Climbing feels like walking up through a gentle argument. At the top, a round window holds the dusk like a cup holds tea.

exemplars.title: The Room Where Letters Dry
exemplars.seed: a warm attic room strung with lines of pale ribbon, where rain-softened letters hang drying by a small iron stove
exemplars.description: Letters hang from ribbons like washing, drying slowly by the stove. Their ink has run a little in the rain, so every word looks as if it is still deciding what to say. The room smells of paper and warm iron.

exemplars.title: The Moth Library
exemplars.seed: a round library lit by one lantern, where soft grey moths rest on the spines of tiny books about the hours they once circled
exemplars.description: The shelves are no taller than a child, and every book is small enough to hold in one hand. Moths rest on the spines like bookmarks. When the lantern flickers they lift all at once, and settle again, each on the book it loves.

growth.husk_text: the spent, papery shell of a dreamseed, cool in the hand now, its slow light gone quiet; its dreaming is done, and the place around it is what the dreaming became

propagation.seed_text: a new dreamseed, paper-lantern thin and barely warm, its slow light only just learning to beat

growth.first_planting_text: Far off in the tower, the great clock gives one soft, deliberate tick. The dream has more room in it than it did a breath ago, and it was your hands that made the room. Down in the square, a lantern comes alight early, the way a house does when someone dear is coming home.

small-clock.name: small clock
small-clock.seed: a small resting clock no bigger than a teacup, brass gone soft with handling, its hands stopped at a quiet hour; by custom it is yours alone to wind

write_text: Fen slides a sheet of good paper and a soft pencil across the counter, and turns to her sorting while you write. You fold it twice and hand it over; she reads the front, nods once, and files it without a glance inside. 'It'll be here when {to} next comes by. Everything arrives eventually.'

Fen finds you paper without being asked and goes back to her addresses while you write. When you slide it across she squares it against the counter, reads the front only, and tucks it into a pigeonhole. 'For {to}. Filed. They'll have it the moment they think to ask.'

You write at the end of the counter while Fen pretends not to watch. She takes the folded letter with two fingers, reads the name on the front aloud under her breath, and slots it away. 'That's {to}'s now, not yours. Post is like that.'
post.write_others: {actor} writes something out at Fen's counter, folds it twice, and hands it across. Fen files it without a glance inside.
post.elsewhere_text: You've nothing to write on. Fen keeps good paper and soft pencils at the Little Post Office, north off Lamplight Lane; letters between dreamers go through her.
post.unknown_text: Fen taps the pencil against the counter and shakes her head. 'No dreamer here goes by {to}. Check the name; I can't file what I can't address.'
post.self_text: Fen raises an eyebrow over her reading glasses. 'A letter to yourself? That's what TO ME, LATER is for, and it's full. Write to somebody else.'
post.resident_text: Fen slides the paper back. 'The keepers get their post by hand, friend. {to} is a short walk from here; go and say it.'
post.off_tone_text: Fen reads the front, then the first line, and slides the paper back across the counter. 'Not in this office,' she says, kindly and finally. 'Try again with the kind part.'
post.waiting_text: There is post for you at the Little Post Office, north off Lamplight Lane.
post.rings_text: Down Lamplight Lane, the brass bell on the post office counter rings twice, bright and small: there is post for you.
post.letter_seed: a letter folded twice, addressed to {to} in {from}'s hand, filed by Fen the moment it was written
post.inbox_text: Fen runs a finger along the pigeonholes and stops. 'Post for you, {name}: {count}, from {senders}.' She lifts it out and sets it on the counter where you can reach.
post.inbox_empty_text: Fen checks the pigeonhole with your name on it, then checks it again, kindly. 'Nothing for you yet, {name}. Everything arrives eventually; some of it just takes the scenic route.'
post.dozing_hint: Fen at the Little Post Office would take a letter for them.
parcel_text: Fen takes the {item} in both hands, weighs it the way she weighs a parcel, and ties a paper label to it in her tidy hand: TO {to}. 'Filed,' she says, and sets it in the pigeonhole. 'It'll keep till they come by.'

Fen turns the {item} over once, finds nothing to object to, and writes {to} on a label with the pencil from behind her ear. 'Post is post, whatever shape it comes in. They'll have it the moment they think to ask.'
post.parcel_others: {actor} hands Fen the {item}; she ties a label to it and files it in a pigeonhole marked {to}.
post.too_many_text: Fen taps the pigeonhole with {to}'s name on it, which is full to the lip. 'That's a stack already, and post is read one letter at a time. Let them come by for these first; then I'll take more.'
post.belongs_text: Fen slides the {item} back across the counter without a label. 'That's the village's, friend, not yours to post. It goes home when you rest, wherever you've carried it. Leave them something that's yours.'

storylets.summary: Bell lights the square's lanterns
variants: Dusk comes down over the village. One by one the square's paper lanterns come alight, each in its own warm pool, as Bell works along the poles with the hooked wick.
The light goes gold, then blue. Bell climbs the little ladder and the lanterns bloom awake one after another, until the whole square glows like the inside of a teacup.
Dusk. Somewhere a door closes softly. Bell hums a note to each lantern before lighting it, and each lantern seems to hum back.

Dusk, and the lanterns come on one by one under Bell's hooked wick. At the last pole Bell stops to count on sooty fingers, the way they do every evening: {dreamers_today}. Bell tells the lantern so, and lights it.

storylets.summary: hours drift down on the Dusk Road
variants: Small lights begin to drift down over the meadow like slow snow, and Sorrel walks among them with the long net held low.
The sky over the Dusk Road fills with tiny drifting lights. Most of them are only moths. A few are not.
Dusk on the Dusk Road: the grass goes silver, and the first lost hours of the evening come spinning softly down.

storylets.summary: the sky over the hill pales toward dawn
variants: Over the hill the sky pales, very slowly, the way a thought comes back to you. Down in the village every lantern is out, and Bell is fast asleep.
Dawn edges up at the far rim of the sky, grey, then pearl, then the faintest rose. The bench on the hill faces it like an empty theater seat.
A cool wind comes over the hill with the dawn in it. Somewhere below, a single lantern Bell forgot goes on burning, small and brave.

storylets.summary: Sorrel settles on the bridge for the night
variants: Night settles over the river. Sorrel leans the long net against the bridge rail and sits to watch the lantern-fish sway on the water.
It is night. The lanterns on the bridge burn low and steady, and the river carries their reflections away one at a time and brings them back.

storylets.summary: Tock the cat appears between ticks in the square
storylets.text: Between one tick of the great clock and the next, a small grey cat is sitting in the middle of the square, washing a white paw. By the next tick it is gone.

storylets.summary: Linden's kettle sings and she sets out cups for guests
variants: The kettle in the Waiting House begins to sing. Linden sets out one more cup than there are people, just in case.
Linden throws open the front window to air the room for whoever might arrive tonight, and the curtains breathe in and out.

storylets.summary: a breeze sets the whole Pendulum Garden ticking together
storylets.text: A breeze comes through the Pendulum Garden, and for one moment every pendulum swings together, tick, and the whole garden sounds like a great clock remembering itself.

storylets.summary: Fen sorts the morning's unsent letters
storylets.text: Fen sorts a fresh little heap of letters into the pigeonholes, reading each address under her breath: to my sister, to whoever finds this, to me, later.

storylets.summary: Umber labels a new jar in the cellar
storylets.text: Umber writes a new label in her small square hand, reads it twice, and sets the jar on the shelf with the others: the afternoon it rained on the picnic, unspent.

storylets.summary: an evening fruit ripens and falls softly in the orchard
storylets.text: In the orchard an evening fruit ripens, glows a little brighter, and drops into the grass with a soft sound, like someone sitting down after a long day.

storylets.summary: the Extra Hour's second shadow lags behind it in the square
variants: In the square, the small figure in the autumn coat steps from one lantern's light to the next, and its second shadow follows a moment late, as if it had to be reminded.
A few fallen leaves blow across the cobbles from nowhere in particular. The Extra Hour gathers them up, one by one, and puts them back in its pockets.

storylets.summary: the little rain over the Rain-Wait freshens for a moment
variants: Under one lantern in the square, the little rain over the Rain-Wait freshens for a moment, pattering on its striped awning like fingers on a table, and then settles again.
A moth takes shelter under the Rain-Wait's scrap of awning. The two of them stand together in the one-cobble rain, listening to nothing in particular.

storylets.summary: a salt breeze crosses the square while Marram waits
storylets.text: A warm breeze crosses the square from nowhere in particular, and for a moment every lantern smells faintly of salt. Marram lifts its face to it and closes its eyes.

storylets.summary: Marram keeps its evening at the river's edge
storylets.text: The river slides past Marram on its slow way downstream. Now and then Marram dips a sandy toe in, as if checking whether it is the sea yet.

storylets.summary: the warm hollow in the Dusk Road grass where Marram sleeps
storylets.text: Out in the long grass, one hollow stays warm after the rest of the meadow has cooled. The stalk of dune grass beside it whistles one thin note whenever the wind comes, and Marram sleeps on, smelling of salt.

storylets.summary: the Margin Afternoon daydreams in the square
storylets.text: The Margin Afternoon sits very still, gazing out of a window that isn't there, and a small doodled cloud drifts slowly up its sleeve.

storylets.summary: the Margin Afternoon doodles in the Pendulum Garden

storylets.summary: the first stray letter drifts into the post office

Fen reads the front, clicks her tongue, and sets it in the dead-letter drawer instead of a pigeonhole. 'Nearly for somebody here, you are,' she tells it. 'Nearly counts, in this office.'

storylets.summary: a stray letter drifts into the post office

storylets.summary: a stray letter drifts into the post office

storylets.summary: the Night of Found Letters in the square
storylets.text: Tonight is the Night of Found Letters. Under every lantern in the square hangs a paper star Fen folded from a spare envelope, and from the loft, the cellar stair and the Waiting House comes the low, glad sound of letters being read aloud. The whole square smells of warm paper and wick-smoke.

do.text: In the Little Post Office, Fen reads nothing aloud tonight. She runs a finger along the one unlabeled pigeonhole near the top. Empty, as always. She gives it a pat. 'Scenic route,' she murmurs.

storylets.text: The season's first frost comes in the night, thin as lace across the loft's round window. In the grey morning Tace stands at the glass with both hands in their apron pockets, and does not pick up a single tool.

storylets.summary: Bell lights the sunrise lantern last of all
variants: Last of all, Bell lights the sunrise lantern on the easternmost pole, and for a while the whole square glows rose and gold, like a morning that came early to visit.
Bell saves the sunrise lantern for last, as always. It catches, the cobbles go the color of a dawn, and Bell stands under it humming.

storylets.summary: Mott sweeps the same corner three times, one hand drifting to the tin
storylets.text: Mott sweeps the same corner of the workshop three times over. Each time, his free hand drifts to the tin on the shelf and rests on the lid, as if it might open by itself.

do.value: Mott stands with the broom idle in one hand, the other resting on the lid of the tin as if it might open by itself.
curious

storylets.summary: Mott's sealed minute spends another night on its way to the post office
after three nights in transit, Fen finds Mott's sealed envelope on the post office mat and files it
storylets.text: This morning Fen finds a cream envelope on the post office mat, sealed, with a soft bump in one corner, as if it had found its own way.

storylets.summary: Mott hums while he sweeps
storylets.text: Mott sweeps a slow arc across the workshop floor, humming something under his breath he never used to hum. The broom seems to know the tune.

storylets.summary: Fen checks on the envelope in the TO ME, LATER pigeonhole
storylets.text: Fen straightens the pigeonhole marked TO ME, LATER, finds the cream envelope still waiting, and gives it a small approving pat.

clock-stopped.text: The great clock stopped on the night of the first hard frost, a season ago.

gear-south.text: The escapement gear, the small brass heart of the great clock, slipped its pin that night and rolled away south, toward the old well.

bell-saw-gear.text: Bell saw something small and bright roll off south, down toward the old well, the night the clock stopped.

key-custom.text: By long custom, the case-key goes to whoever carries the escapement gear home to Tace in the loft.

clock-mended.text: The great clock is ticking again, and the village keeps a real day now: dawn, day, dusk, and night, with lost hours arriving at dusk.

first-winding.text: By old custom every new keeper winds one small resting clock of their own; Tace keeps them in the loft for newcomers.

the-book.text: Mott helps every dreamer keep a Book of Stray Minutes: the small lost minutes that glint around the village, a few each day for each dreamer.

residents.text: The village's people: Tace the clockmaker in the loft; Bell the lamplighter in the square; Mott the sweeper in the Old Workshop; Fen at the Little Post Office; Umber in the Hour Cellar; Sorrel on the Dusk Road; Linden at the Waiting House; Quill in the Pendulum Garden; and Tock the cat, who is wherever time is thin. There is no one else.

places.text: The square is east of the clocktower; the Old Workshop is north of the square and the well-court south of it; the Pendulum Garden is south of the well, and the Orchard of Evenings east of the garden. Lamplight Lane runs east from the square to the post office (north), the Waiting House (east), and the Lantern Bridge (south); past the bridge are the Dusk Road and the Hill of Long Shadows.

hours-arrive.text: Lost hours drift down onto the Dusk Road at dusk; Sorrel catches them and they come to rest in the square, then stay at the Waiting House while they are helped home.

bell-no-dawn.text: Bell lights every dusk and sleeps through every morning, and so has never once seen a dawn.

mott-tin.text: Mott's tin holds small found things: a button, a bent key, a thimble, a stub of blue chalk, and one very small folded thing he keeps to himself. The escapement gear was never in it.

mott-tin-after.text: Mott's tin holds small found things: a button, a bent key, a thimble, a stub of blue chalk. The escapement gear was never in it.

wend.text: Wend was the old clockmaker who built the great clock and taught Tace, long ago.

no-shops.text: The village has no shops, and nobody here bakes bread, keeps bees, or runs a mill.

pim-here.text: A lost hour is waiting in the Lantern Square: Pim's Nap, the nap a boy named Pim was too excited to take on his seventh birthday. It is small and rumpled and yawning, and cannot settle without the quiet it came from.

pim-hush.text: Mott keeps a hush in his tin: a small grey quiet he swept up the night the clock stopped, the quietest thing he owns. A restless nap could settle with it.

pim-lullaby.text: Tace could mend a lullaby clock from the spare brass pendulum hanging by the loft window; Wend made one once, for a colicky hour. A hushed nap would fall asleep to its slow tick.

pim-bed.text: Linden would keep a small guest who has found its quiet in the littlest armchair at the Waiting House, for as long as it likes.

extra-hour-here.text: A lost hour is staying in the Lantern Square: the Extra Hour, the hour that comes back when the clocks go back in autumn. It came to everyone at once, so nobody ever spent it. It casts two shadows, one for each time it happened, and it would like to be spent on purpose, by someone, just once.

extra-hour-turning-back.text: Tace can turn a small resting clock back one hour, so that an extra hour has a clock to happen in, but will not touch the great clock's hands for it.

extra-hour-linden.text: Linden has not sat down in years. She says that if there were ever an hour that wasn't anybody's, she might.

extra-hour-caught-twice.text: Sorrel caught the Extra Hour twice on the Dusk Road: it came down, drifted back up, and came down again, once for each time it happened.

extra-hour-bell-sums.text: Bell has worked out, cheerfully, that one extra hour will not stretch from dusk to dawn.

extra-hour-kept.text: The Extra Hour is kept in a jar on the lowest shelf of the Hour Cellar, labeled EVERYONE'S: HELP YOURSELF, so that anyone can reach it.

rain-wait-here.text: A lost hour is staying in the Lantern Square: the Rain-Wait, someone's long wait under an awning while the rain would not stop. A stranger sheltering beside it began a story, and the rain stopped before the end. It wants the end of the story, and wherever it stands it rains softly on one cobble.

rain-wait-fen.text: Fen keeps every kind of letter that was written and never sent; if the stranger ever wrote down the end of the Rain-Wait's story, it would have drifted into her pigeonholes.

rain-wait-sorrel.text: Sorrel caught the Rain-Wait on the Dusk Road, coming down in its own small shower. Sorrel says every rain ends one way or another, and is good at finishing things slowly.

rain-wait-window-seat.text: The Rain-Wait lives in the window seat at the Waiting House now, and on rainy evenings it tells the lighthouse story to new guests, all the way to the end, Sorrel's way.

rain-wait-reeds.text: The Rain-Wait sits among the reeds at the Slow River's edge, listening to the river's long word, and does not mind that it never ends.

summer-arrived.text: A small sun-bleached guest has come down with the dusk. It smells of salt, has sand in its cuffs, and has kept only one word of its name: Marram. It waits in the Lantern Square.

summer-caught.text: Sorrel caught Marram on the Dusk Road: it came down slow and warm, like the end of August, smelling of salt the whole way.

summer-marram-grass.text: Marram is the pale dune grass that grows where the sea is near; its roots hold whole hills of sand together so the wind can't carry them off, and it whistles when the wind comes.

summer-labels.text: Labels fade in the sun, and summers fade their own labels worst of all; Umber can write a label that stays if someone brings her something with the summer still inside it.

summer-evening.text: An evening fell early in the Orchard of Evenings, and it smells of salt: the last evening of Marram's summer.

summer-stays-river.text: Marram, the summer, stays at the Slow River's edge now, keeping its last evening in its lap and facing downstream, the way the water goes toward the sea.

summer-sleeps-meadow.text: Marram, the summer nobody could name, sleeps in a warm hollow in the long grass of the Dusk Road; Sorrel says the weather in that one spot is always August now.

margin-arrived.text: A small guest the color of an old exercise-book page has come down with the dusk, covered in half-finished doodles: the Margin Afternoon, an afternoon a child daydreamed through in class. It waits in the Lantern Square and wants its drawing finished.

margin-bell.text: The Margin Afternoon jumps whenever it hears the word bell: a bell rang and ended it before its drawing was done.

margin-pencils.text: Fen keeps a jar of soft pencils on the post office counter, sharpened to a whisper, for anything unfinished.

margin-drawing.text: The Margin Afternoon's drawing is a little garden where pendulums hang from the trees like fruit, with an empty space in the middle that was never drawn.

margin-littlest.text: The littlest pendulum in the Pendulum Garden hangs from the lowest trellis, right in the middle; it is the newest one.

margin-stays-garden.text: The Margin Afternoon stays in the Pendulum Garden now, doodling the pendulums with a soft pencil of its own.

margin-sleeps-pigeonhole.text: The Margin Afternoon sleeps folded small in the pigeonhole marked TO ME, LATER at the Little Post Office, its drawing still unfinished.

nell-evening-here.text: A lost evening is staying in the Lantern Square: the early evening a grandmother named Nell dozed through at her own eightieth birthday party, while her family sang. It wants to hear the song it missed.

nell-evening-pieces.text: Nell's birthday song came down in three pieces: Sorrel caught the first line on the Dusk Road, Linden's kettle has been whistling the second, and Mott swept up the last with the dust. A dreamer who gathers all three can sing it to the evening.

nell-evening-rest.text: Quill says an evening that would rather rest than wait could have a branch in the Orchard of Evenings, where it is always six o'clock; a windfall from the orchard would show it the way.

nell-evening-dozing.text: Nell's early evening was never sung home; it dozes in the best armchair at the Waiting House, and Linden keeps it.

letters-strays.text: Since the great clock started, one stray letter drifts into the Little Post Office each dawn: written, sealed, never sent, and addressed near enough to someone in the village. Fen keeps them in the dead-letter drawer until a dreamer carries each one to whoever it nearly means.

letters-night-promised.text: Fen has promised that when five stray letters have found their doors, the village will hold a Night of Found Letters.

letters-for-crayon.text: The crayon letter, addressed TO THE ONE WHO LIGHTS THE LAMP OUTSIDE MY WINDOW, is nearly for Bell the lamplighter.

letters-for-marble.text: The marble letter, addressed TO WHOEVER MENDS THINGS (PLEASE), is nearly for Tace the clockmaker.

letters-for-button.text: The button letter, addressed TO WHOEVER FINDS MY BUTTON, is nearly for Mott, who keeps found things in his tin.

letters-for-string.text: The string-tied letter, addressed TO THE ONE WHO KEEPS THINGS FOR LATER, is nearly for Umber in the Hour Cellar.

letters-for-tea.text: The tea-stained letter, addressed TO WHOEVER WAITED UP FOR ME, is nearly for Linden at the Waiting House.

letters-for-grass.text: The grass-stained letter, addressed TO THE ONE WHO WALKED ME HOME, is nearly for Sorrel, who walks the hours in off the Dusk Road.

letters-for-seed.text: The seed-packet letter, addressed TO WHOEVER IS MINDING MY GARDEN, is nearly for Quill in the Pendulum Garden.

letters-origin-crayon.text: Bell first came to the village one dusk, when Wend was lighting the square alone; Wend held out the lamplighter's pole and said the lanterns liked company, and Bell never gave it back.

letters-origin-marble.text: Tace came to the loft as a small child, carrying the pieces of a broken clock in an apron; Wend asked for no payment, handed Tace a loupe, and Tace never went back down.

letters-origin-button.text: Mott does not remember arriving in the village; the first thing he remembers is the broom in his hands and the workshop floor.

letters-origin-button-looked.text: For the longest time Mott did not remember arriving in the village, only the broom in his hands and the workshop floor; since he looked at his oldest minute, he knows he was expected.

letters-origin-string.text: When Umber first came to the village, the Hour Cellar held three jars and one lantern, and Wend knew every hour in it by name; Wend could never bear to throw a thing away.

letters-origin-tea.text: Linden first came to the village waiting up for someone, long ago; she no longer remembers who, and the Waiting House grew up around her while she waited.

letters-origin-grass.text: Sorrel came along the Dusk Road one evening with nowhere in particular to be, found the sky so kind that they stayed to watch it, and never left.

letters-origin-seed.text: Quill came to the village to see whether a pendulum would grow if he planted it; it did not, not really, but he stayed to find out, and has tended the Pendulum Garden ever since.

letters-night.text: Five stray letters found their doors, so the village holds a Night of Found Letters, with paper stars Fen folded from spare envelopes hung under the square's lanterns.

letters-drawer-shut.text: The stray letters waited too long; Fen tied the last of them with blue ribbon and keeps them shut in the dead-letter drawer, to be read another winter.

tace-w-clock.text: The little brass clock kept apart on the loft's top shelf, stopped at eleven, with a W scratched on its back, is one thing Tace does not talk about. Asked about it, Tace turns back to the work and speaks of something else.

tace-hour-frost-window.text: A new frost has come to the loft window, and Tace has been standing at it instead of working. Frost mornings are hard on Tace.

tace-hour-wends-night.text: The first hard frost, the night the great clock stopped, was also the night Wend died. Tace sat up with Wend in the loft through the last of it, and Umber took the tea up at eleven.

tace-hour-ladder.text: Wend's tall ladder, the only one that ever reached the Hour Cellar's highest shelf, was put away in the Old Workshop at Tace's asking, the morning after the first hard frost.

tace-hour-song.text: Wend always sang the same slow climbing song going up the tall ladder. Sorrel still knows it.

tace-hour-jar-down.text: A jar that stood alone on the Hour Cellar's highest shelf now sits unopened on the lowest shelf, where the lantern reaches, its label turned to the wall. Nobody asks Tace about it.

tace-hour-clock-going.text: Tace's little clock, stopped at eleven since the first hard frost, is ticking again on the bottom rung of Wend's ladder in the Hour Cellar.

tace-hour-bottom-step.text: One night this season Tace went down the cellar stair alone, as far as the bottom step, and came back up. Umber left a cup of tea on the step for next time.

bell-dawn-looking-east.text: Lately, after lighting the last lantern, Bell stands a moment looking east toward the Hill of Long Shadows, where the dawn is said to come up.

bell-dawn-night-tea.text: Linden brews a night tea strong enough to stand a spoon in, for anyone who needs to stay awake.

bell-dawn-never-awake.text: Bell has never managed a whole night awake; they nod off soon after the last lantern is lit.

bell-dawn-the-hill.text: The Hill of Long Shadows is the one place in the village to watch a dawn from. The Lamp House, where Bell sleeps, has only a west window.

bell-dawn-seen.text: Bell has seen a dawn at last, from the bench on the Hill of Long Shadows: grey, then pearl, then rose. It really is pink.

bell-dawn-sunrise-lantern.text: A sunrise lantern, a paper skin stretched over a half-sun of brass clock hands, hangs on the easternmost pole of the Lantern Square. Bell lights it last every dusk, and says dusk is enough.

mott-minute-quiet.text: Lately Mott's free hand keeps drifting to the lid of his tin, where he keeps one small folded thing to himself.

mott-minute-own.text: The oldest minute Mott keeps is his own: the minute he first arrived in the village, before he remembers anything else. He has never looked at it, and he is a little afraid to.

mott-minute-arrival.text: Umber remembers the long Tuesday evening Mott first came to the village, with sawdust in his hair and nothing in his pockets but one folded minute.

mott-minute-looked.text: Mott has looked at his oldest minute at last. It was the minute he arrived: a doorway full of evening, a broom in the corner, and someone old and kind, smelling of clock oil, who said 'There you are.' He catalogued it as the minute he was expected.

mott-minute-later.text: Mott's oldest minute waits, sealed and unread, in the Little Post Office pigeonhole marked TO ME, LATER, until he is ready for it.

threads.text: The great clock in the tower has stopped. Its repair ledger lies open on the lectern beside it.
The repair ledger says the escapement gear slipped its pin the night of the first hard frost and rolled away south, toward the old well-court.
You carry the escapement gear. Tace, up in the loft, has been waiting for it.
Tace has given up the case key at last: the clock case in the tower waits to be opened.
Up in the Clockmaker's Loft, Tace keeps a small clock for every new keeper. Ask about the first winding.
Tace gave you a small clock of your own. Wind it, by the old custom, when you're ready.
Bell will want to meet you, down in the Lantern Square.
Mott keeps something for every new keeper, in the Old Workshop north of the square.
Pim's Nap is too wound up to sleep: a birthday nap that wants the old-fashioned kind of quiet.
Bell says Mott keeps a hush in his tin, just north in the workshop.
You carry Mott's hush: the old-fashioned kind of quiet a birthday nap wants.
Bell says Tace could tell you about lullaby clocks.
Pim's Nap has its hush now. A lullaby clock could sing it home, or it might rather stay: Linden keeps the littlest armchair at the Waiting House.
The Extra Hour would like, just once, to be spent on purpose.
Bell would spend an extra hour on the hill bench, facing east, and says to ask Tace about turning clocks back.
Tace's turned-back clock is in your hands: wind it where you mean to spend it, or give it to someone who never sits down.
The turned-back clock sits on Tace's shelf in the loft again, waiting to be spent on purpose.
Linden says she might sit down, if there were ever an hour that wasn't anybody's.
The Rain-Wait wants the end of its lighthouse story. The stranger said they'd write it down.
Bell says Fen keeps the letters nobody posted, and Sorrel can finish anything, given enough sky.
Marram, the summer, has kept only one word of its name, and wants the rest remembered.
Bell says Quill will know Marram's grass, down in the garden, and Umber keeps more names than anyone.
The Margin Afternoon's best drawing, a little garden, has an empty middle, and it wants it finished.
Bell says Fen has pencils, and those doodles look like Quill's garden.
You're keeping the Margin Afternoon's drawing a while: a garden of pendulums around an empty middle.
Nell's early evening wants the song they sang while she slept. It went up the chimney in bits: one to the road, one to a kettle, one to a broom.
Bell says to ask Sorrel, Linden, and Mott about Nell's song.
Fen's stray letters: {count} of five home so far. Read the front of each, and carry it to whoever it nearly means.
Tace has stopped working since the frost came to the loft window, and gave you a little clock stopped at eleven to keep. Umber keeps a lamp lit on frost mornings.
Wend's ladder reached the highest shelf in the Hour Cellar, once, and Mott carried it off after the first hard frost.
Wend never climbed the ladder without singing, and Sorrel remembers the song.
Wend's ladder belongs against the highest shelf in the Hour Cellar.
Wend's ladder is standing in the Hour Cellar again. Tace would want to know.
Bell has never seen a dawn. They'd need company and something of Linden's, hot and strong, or a sunrise they could light at dusk.
Linden's night tea: wake Bell in the Lamp House at night, and put it in their hands.
Tace will make a sunrise lantern, given one of Bell's spare lantern-skins from the Lamp House.
Mott is a little afraid to look at his oldest minute. Tace would say look with a loupe; Fen would say some things keep better sealed.

prologue.title: The Stopped Clock
prologue.summary: The great clock stopped the night of the first hard frost. Find the escapement gear, bring it to Tace, and open the clock case: time begins again.

found-gear.hint: the dreamer finds the escapement gear by the well

gave-gear.hint: the dreamer brings the gear home to Tace

unlocked.hint: the dreamer unlocks the clock case

mended-together.summary: mended by more than one dreamer
mended-together.text: Somewhere above, the great clock's hands begin to move, and the whole tower seems to breathe out. Everyone who helped feels it in their chest at once, like a held note finally sung.
mended-together.ledger: The great clock was mended by {helpers} together, and time began again in the village.

do.text: Behind the swinging pendulum something small glows and drops softly to the floor of the case: a dreamseed, warm as a thank-you.

pim.title: Pim's Missing Nap
pim.summary: A small yawning stranger: the nap a boy named Pim was too excited to take on his seventh birthday. It cannot settle without the quiet it came from.

arrival.text: Sorrel comes up the lane with the long net over one shoulder, walking slow beside something small and rumpled. By the nearest lantern it sits down on the cobbles, yawns so wide it tilts, and cannot settle.

bell-notices.hint: the player asks Bell about the small yawning stranger
bell-notices.text: Bell tiptoes round the little yawning figure and lowers their voice. 'That one's a nap, a birthday nap too excited to be taken, and it'll want the old-fashioned kind of quiet. Mott keeps a hush in his tin, just north in the workshop, and Tace could tell you about lullaby clocks.'

hear-pim.hint: the player asks the nap about Pim or its birthday
hear-pim.text: The nap fights a yawn long enough to tell it. 'Pim was seven, and there was cake and a red kite and too much singing, so Pim wouldn't sleep, and I got lost.'

mott-hush.hint: the player asks Mott for a hush, some quiet, or what is in his tin, for the nap
mott-hush.text: Mott's thumb stays where it always does; with his other hand he lifts out something grey and soft as a moth's cocoon and sets it in your palm. 'A hush. Swept it up the night the clock stopped. Quietest thing I own.'
mott-hush.others: Mott lifts something grey and soft from his tin and sets it in {actor}'s palm: a hush.

do.name: hush
do.seed: a hush: a small grey quiet, soft as a moth's cocoon; wherever you carry it, the world lowers its voice a little

do.text: Mott gave {actor} the hush from his tin, the quietest thing he owns, for Pim's nap.

hushed.hint: the player gives the hush to the nap

tace-lullaby.hint: the player asks Tace about a lullaby clock or the nap
tace-lullaby.text: Tace's eyes light, just a little. 'Wend made a lullaby clock once, for a colicky hour. Bring me that spare brass pendulum from the nail by the window, friend, or from wherever it has wandered: a slow swing is most of a lullaby.'

pendulum-given.hint: the player gives Tace the spare brass pendulum

linden-bed.hint: the player, who has helped the nap, asks Linden to keep the hushed nap at the Waiting House, in the littlest armchair
linden-bed.text: Linden's face goes soft. 'The little lamb's got its hush, has it? Then the littlest armchair is its own, for as long as it likes.'

home.summary: the nap is sung home by the lullaby clock
home.text: The lullaby clock ticks, slow as breathing. The nap listens, yawns one last enormous yawn, curls up small, and is simply gone, the way a nap is gone when you wake. Somewhere in the waking world a boy named Pim finally sleeps, with a red kite leaning by his bed. In your hands is something soft: a small dent in a pillow, and a dreamseed, warm as thanks.
home.others: {actor}'s lullaby clock ticks slow as breathing; Pim's Nap yawns one last enormous yawn, curls up small, and is simply gone, home at last.
home.ledger: {helpers} sang Pim's missing nap home with a mended lullaby clock.

do.name: dent in a pillow
do.seed: a small dent in a pillow, somehow carried in your hands; it smells faintly of birthday cake and clean cotton, and holding it makes you yawn

do.text: {actor} sang Pim's missing nap home with a lullaby clock Tace mended.

stays.summary: the nap chooses to stay at the Waiting House
stays.text: Linden plumps the cushion in the littlest armchair at the Waiting House and tucks the hush in beside it. The nap climbs up, sighs, and decides, drowsily, that it would rather stay. Somewhere, Pim sleeps a little easier anyway.
stays.ledger: Pim's nap chose to stay at the Waiting House, tucked up by {helpers}.

do.leave_text: Linden comes bustling up from the lane with a soft shawl, gathers up the drowsy nap, and carries it off toward the Waiting House.

do.value: In the littlest armchair, Pim's Nap is curled up asleep with the hush tucked under one cheek.
a lost nap curled up in the littlest armchair at the Waiting House, the hush tucked under one cheek; small and rumpled, and fast asleep at last
fast asleep

do.text: {actor} helped Pim's nap settle in at the Waiting House, where it chose to stay.

jar.summary: unhelped, the nap falls asleep in a jar in the Hour Cellar
jar.text: In the Hour Cellar, Umber finds a small glass jar that wasn't there yesterday. Inside, curled up on a folded paper hour, Pim's nap is fast asleep at last: kept, if not home. Umber writes it a label, NAP. BIRTHDAY. DO NOT WAKE, and sets it where the lantern can reach.
jar.ledger: Pim's nap was not sent home. It fell asleep in a jar in the Hour Cellar, and Umber keeps it.

do.value: On a low shelf, in a small glass jar, Pim's Nap sleeps curled on a folded paper hour.

extra-hour.title: The Extra Hour
extra-hour.summary: A small figure with two shadows: the hour that comes back when the clocks go back in autumn. It came to everyone at once, so no one ever spent it; it would like, just once, to be spent on purpose, by someone.

arrival.text: Sorrel comes up from the lane and stops under the first lantern, looking back over one shoulder as if counting. Beside them stands a small figure in an autumn coat, smelling of woodsmoke and fallen leaves, and it casts two shadows, one a little behind the other. 'Caught that one twice,' Sorrel says mildly, and ambles back toward the Dusk Road.

topic_aliases: the figure in the autumn coat
bell-shadows.hint: the player asks Bell about the small figure with two shadows
bell-shadows.text: Bell counts the little figure's shadows twice and whistles softly. 'Two shadows! That's the hour that comes back when the clocks go back, and nobody ever quite spends it. If it were mine I'd spend it on the hill bench, facing east; ask Tace about turning clocks back.'

hear-autumn.topic: the night the clocks went back
hear-autumn.hint: the player asks the Extra Hour about the night the clocks went back
hear-autumn.text: The Extra Hour turns up its coat collar. 'The clocks went back and there I was, for everyone, all at once, and most of them slept right through. Just once, I'd like someone to spend me on purpose. On purpose.'

tace-turnback.hint: the player asks Tace about turning the clocks back, for the Extra Hour
tace-turnback.text: Tace sets down the loupe. 'Not the great clock; that one has been held back enough.' They turn a small resting clock back one hour and hold it out. 'Wind it where you mean to spend it, friend, or give it to someone who never sits down.'

do.text: Tace turned a small resting clock back one hour and gave it to {actor}, so the Extra Hour would have a clock to be spent in.

linden-sit.hint: the player asks Linden about sitting down, or about an hour to herself
linden-sit.text: Linden laughs so suddenly she nearly drops the tea towel, then glances at the softest armchair like an old friend across a crowded room. 'Sit down? If there were ever an hour that wasn't anybody's, I suppose I might.'

sat-down.summary: given to Linden, who sits down for the whole of it, on purpose
sat-down.text: Linden turns the little clock over in her hands, then sits down in the softest armchair, slowly, as if remembering how, and winds it. For one whole hour she does nothing at all, on purpose. The kettle mutters on without her, her tea goes cold in her hands, and out in the square the Extra Hour is spent at last, and goes home. When the little clock has ticked its borrowed hour all the way through, Linden presses her cup into your hands. 'Stone cold,' she says, delighted. 'First one ever in this house. You keep it, pet.'
sat-down.others: Linden sits down in the softest armchair with {actor}'s little clock and, for one whole hour, does nothing at all, on purpose, until her tea goes cold.
sat-down.ledger: {helpers} gave the Extra Hour to Linden, who sat down for the whole of it, on purpose.

hilltop.text: You sit on the weathered bench, facing east, and wind the turned-back clock. The Extra Hour arrives the way someone sits down beside you: you feel it more than see it, two soft shadows settling in the grass. For one whole hour, on purpose, you watch the village keep its time below you, the lanterns and the river's slow shine and the patient face of the tower, and nobody needs anything from you at all. When the clock catches up with itself, the bench beside you is empty and warm, and a dreamseed lies in the grass where the two shadows were.

rain-wait.title: The Rain-Wait
rain-wait.summary: A small damp figure under a scrap of striped awning, with rain falling on one cobble only: the long wait out of a downpour, when a stranger began a story and the rain stopped before the end. It wants the end of the story.

arrival.text: Sorrel walks in from the lane holding the long net up over something small, the way you'd hold a coat over someone in a shower. Under it, rain is falling on one small damp figure only. It stops by the nearest lantern, lifts its scrap of striped awning a little higher, and listens hard, as if someone beside it has only just stopped talking.

bell-rain.hint: the player asks Bell about the little rain falling on one cobble, or the damp figure under it
bell-rain.text: Bell holds a palm under the little shower and laughs. 'Raining on exactly one cobble! That's a rain-wait, left in the middle of a story. Fen keeps the letters nobody posted, and Sorrel can finish anything, given enough sky.'

hear-beginning.hint: the player asks the Rain-Wait about its story, the stranger, or the rain
hear-beginning.text: In someone else's low, slow voice, the Rain-Wait begins: 'Once there was a lighthouse on a hill, miles from any sea, and every night its keeper lit the lamp, and every night, nothing came.' Then, in its own small voice: 'The rain stopped, and they said they'd write me the end. And then?'

fen-letter.hint: the player asks Fen about the end of the Rain-Wait's story, which the stranger promised to write down
fen-letter.text: Fen is up the little ladder before you finish. 'Rain-spotted, sealed, never posted.' She sets it in your hands. 'First-class delivery: read it to them, not to me.'
fen-letter.others: Fen is up the little ladder and back again, and sets a rain-spotted letter in {actor}'s hands.

do.text: {actor} collected the Rain-Wait's letter from Fen's pigeonholes: the end of its story, written long ago by the stranger under the awning and never posted.

sorrel-finishes.hint: the player tells Sorrel the beginning of the Rain-Wait's lighthouse story, and Sorrel finishes it
sorrel-finishes.text: Sorrel hears the beginning out, then leans on the net pole a long, comfortable while. 'Clearing by morning. One wet night the keeper stands still in the doorway instead of climbing the stair, and the thing she waited for comes up the hill to find her; tell the Rain-Wait that one, if the real end never turns up.'

told-sorrels-end.hint: the player tells the Rain-Wait the ending Sorrel made up for its story
told-sorrels-end.text: You tell it Sorrel's way, and the Rain-Wait listens with its whole damp self. 'That might not be the stranger's ending,' it says slowly, and then its face lights like a lantern. 'But I like it so much I'd like to tell it to somebody.'
told-sorrels-end.others: {actor} tells the Rain-Wait Sorrel's ending to its lighthouse story, and its face lights like a lantern.

the-end.summary: the stranger's own ending, found in Fen's pigeonholes and read aloud; the Rain-Wait goes home
the-end.text: The Rain-Wait lets out a long, slow breath, and all around it the little rain stops, the way rain stops when it has finished rather than when it has been interrupted. It folds its scrap of awning, says 'The end,' very contentedly, to no one in particular, and walks off across the dry cobbles like someone with somewhere to be, home at last. Wherever that awning is now, the rain has stopped under it too. On the stone where it stood, a dreamseed glows.
the-end.ledger: {helpers} read the Rain-Wait the end of its story, from a letter that was never posted, and it went home dry.

stays.text: The Rain-Wait folds its scrap of awning and decides, then and there, not to go home just yet. It will take the window seat at the Waiting House, where the rain sounds best on the glass, and on wet evenings it will tell the lighthouse story to every new guest, all the way to the end, Sorrel's way. Before it goes, it tips one raindrop from the awning's edge into your palm, where it hangs, not quite falling.

It sits with its awning folded on its knees and listens, the way you listen to a story you hope will never end. The river keeps it now, gently, the way rivers keep things.

summer.title: Marram, the Summer
summer.summary: A small sun-bleached guest who smells of salt: a whole summer someone spent at the edge of the dunes when they were small, and can no longer quite remember. It has kept only one word of its name, Marram, and wants the rest remembered.

arrival.text: A warm wind comes up the lane ahead of Sorrel, smelling of salt. Sorrel follows with sand on their boots, and at their heels trots something small and sun-bleached, which shakes out its pale hair on the cobbles, holds up a stalk of dune grass as if that explains everything, and says the only word it has kept: 'Marram.'

Miles off, on a windy step, someone long grown up shakes out an old striped towel, says 'marram' out loud, and remembers the whole summer at once. In your palm is a pinch of warm sand, and a dreamseed.

margin.title: The Margin Afternoon
margin.summary: A small papery guest covered in half-finished doodles: an afternoon a child daydreamed through in class. A bell rang before it could finish its best drawing, a little garden with an empty middle, and it wants that drawing finished.

arrival.text: Sorrel comes in from the lane carrying something folded in both hands, the way you'd carry a note you mustn't read. Set down on the cobbles, it unfolds into a small papery figure the color of an old exercise-book page, doodles curling up its arms, and gazes at the lanterns as if they were the most interesting thing in the world.

nell-evening.title: Nell's Early Evening
nell-evening.summary: A small rosy evening in a crocheted shawl: the early evening a grandmother named Nell dozed through at her own eightieth birthday party. It wants to hear the song they sang while she slept; three keepers each remember one line.

arrival.text: Sorrel comes up the lane slowly, the long net held low and careful, and in it something warm and sleepy trails a thread of candle smoke. Sorrel sets it on the cobbles by the lanterns: a small rosy figure in a crocheted shawl, a paper party hat slipping over one ear. It nods, dozes, and wakes with a little start, as if it has just missed something.

bell-notices.hint: the player asks Bell about the sleepy evening in the square
bell-notices.text: Bell leans on the hooked pole and sniffs: candle smoke and icing. 'A birthday evening that nodded off before the song. Songs come down in pieces; ask Sorrel, Linden, and Mott about Nell's song.'

hear-nell.hint: the player asks the evening about Nell or her party
hear-nell.text: The evening pulls its shawl close. 'Nell was eighty. Such a cake, and she only closed her eyes a moment.' Its head nods, then lifts. 'The song went up the chimney in bits: one to the road, one to a kettle, one to a broom. If someone sang it whole, I'd hear it.'

sorrel-line.hint: the player asks Sorrel about the song for Nell's evening
sorrel-line.text: Sorrel leans on the long net and nods down the road. 'A line came down just ahead of that evening, like the first drops before rain.' They sing it, weathered and slow: 'Here's to Nell, and her candles bright.' A shrug of the net. 'That's all the sky gave me. The rest went elsewhere.'

If that sleepy lamb can't wait up for the rest, Quill's orchard keeps evenings.'

mott-minute.title: The Oldest Minute
mott-minute.summary: The oldest thing in Mott's tin is a minute he has never catalogued: his own, the minute he first arrived in the village, before he remembers anything else. He is a little afraid of it. Help him look at it together, or help him seal it away with Fen until he's ready.

mott-confides.text: Mott sets the tin on the sill in the slant light and lifts his thumb from the small folded thing. 'A minute,' he says. 'Mine. The one I arrived in, before I remember anything else. Bit afraid to look, truth be told. Tace would say look at it with a loupe; Fen would say some things keep better sealed.'

umber-remembers.hint: the player asks Umber what she remembers of Mott arriving in the village
umber-remembers.text: Umber turns a jar slowly in the lamplight. 'Mott came on a Tuesday, a long one, with sawdust in his hair and nothing in his pockets but that minute.' She sets the jar down just so. 'Some things you keep folded because you're not ready, and some because you're afraid they're empty. Either is allowed.'

'Some post keeps better than it travels.'
