collectibles.name: the night-before minute
collectibles.text: the night before a birthday, far too awake to sleep, guessing at a rustle of paper downstairs

collectibles.name: the wet-paint minute
collectibles.text: a door freshly painted, a sign saying so, and one small finger that had to check

collectibles.name: the almost-said minute
collectibles.text: the thing you meant to say, very nearly said, and a remark about the weather instead

collectibles.name: the nearly-landed minute
collectibles.text: a butterfly that nearly landed on an outstretched hand, and chose a flower instead

collectibles.name: the jelly minute
collectibles.text: a jelly in a bowl, not set yet, and a small face checking on it every few minutes

collectibles.name: the egg-timer minute
collectibles.text: an egg timer's last few grains of sand, sliding through one by one

collectibles.name: the floating minute
collectibles.text: the first time the water held you up, after letting go of the riverbank

collectibles.name: the sorry minute
collectibles.text: a sorry said first, though it was not really your fault, and the room softening

collectibles.name: the landing minute
collectibles.text: a dark landing crossed all alone, which turned out to be only a landing after all

collectibles.name: the new-classroom minute
collectibles.text: a new classroom full of strange faces, and a 'hello' said anyway

collectibles.name: the high-branch minute
collectibles.text: one branch higher than ever before, a look down, and a quick look back up

collectibles.name: the solo minute
collectibles.text: a song's opening note, sung alone in front of everyone before the voice had warmed up

collectibles.name: the asking minute
collectibles.text: a shy 'would you like to dance?', answered yes before it was even finished

collectibles.name: the spider-and-cup minute
collectibles.text: a spider carried out to the garden under a teacup and a postcard, very gently

collectibles.name: the owning-up minute
collectibles.text: the broken vase, owned up to before anyone had even asked

collectibles.name: the sit-beside minute
collectibles.text: an empty seat beside someone eating lunch alone, taken with a smile

collectibles.name: the cold-sea minute
collectibles.text: a run straight into the cold sea, all at once, because slowly was worse

collectibles.name: the splinter minute
collectibles.text: a splinter eased out of a thumb, a face held very still, and hardly any crying

collectibles.name: the shut-door minute
collectibles.text: bedtime with the door closed all the way for the very first time, and sleep coming anyway

collectibles.name: the one-line minute
collectibles.text: one line to say in the school play, gone completely, then back just in time

collectibles.name: the lamplighting minute
collectibles.text: a single lamp lit in a darkening room, and the windows turning into mirrors

collectibles.name: the cricket minute
collectibles.text: one cricket starting up in the long grass, and then all of them

collectibles.name: the back-step minute
collectibles.text: a back step after supper, and nothing at all left to do

collectibles.name: the warm-towel minute
collectibles.text: a towel warmed by the fire, wrapped round someone small straight out of the bath

collectibles.name: the lullaby minute
collectibles.text: a lullaby's last verse, sung slower and slower as the eyes closed

collectibles.name: the extra-story minute
collectibles.text: the extra story, pleaded for and granted, which turned out to be the longest on the shelf

collectibles.name: the first-star minute
collectibles.text: the first star, and a wish made on it before anyone else could

collectibles.name: the music-box minute
collectibles.text: a music box winding down, its tune growing slower and sleepier until it stopped mid-note

collectibles.name: the warm-spot minute
collectibles.text: cold feet finding the warm place where the stone bottle had been

collectibles.name: the goodnights minute
collectibles.text: goodnight said to every room in the house on the way up to bed

collectibles.name: the ember minute
collectibles.text: the embers of the fire building little towns and letting them fall

collectibles.name: the humming minute
collectibles.text: someone humming over the dishes in the next room, the tune coming and going

collectibles.name: the supper minute
collectibles.text: everyone at the supper table at once, all talking, and all of it lovely

collectibles.name: the fiddle minute
collectibles.text: a fiddle tune drifting up the lane from somewhere on a summer evening

collectibles.name: the swift minute
collectibles.text: the blue minute after sunset, when the swifts came down low over the rooftops, calling

collectibles.name: the last-bell minute
collectibles.text: the last bell on the last day of school, and everyone suddenly quiet

collectibles.name: the empty-room minute
collectibles.text: an empty room on moving day, and a goodbye said to the marks on the wall

collectibles.name: the waving minute
collectibles.text: a friend walking away down the lane, turning back to wave, and then once more

collectibles.name: the outgrown minute
collectibles.text: a favourite pair of shoes that no longer fitted, put away kindly at the back of the cupboard

collectibles.name: the open-hands minute
collectibles.text: cupped hands opened for a mended sparrow, which flew off without once looking back

collectibles.name: the hand-me-down minute
collectibles.text: a much-loved coat handed down to someone smaller, and the way it fitted them

collectibles.name: the last-page minute
collectibles.text: a book nobody wanted to end, down to its very last page

collectibles.name: the snowman minute
collectibles.text: the snowman's hat sliding off in the thaw, and everyone agreeing it had been a very good snowman

collectibles.name: the armchair minute
collectibles.text: a grandfather's armchair, sat in for the first time, and still the shape of him

collectibles.name: the last-look minute
collectibles.text: one last look back from the garden gate at a holiday cottage, its shutters already closed

collectibles.name: the last-swim minute
collectibles.text: the last swim of the summer, the water a little colder than the day before

collectibles.name: the suitcase minute
collectibles.text: an evening in a house by the sea, the last one, with the suitcases waiting by the door

collectibles.name: the last-lullaby minute
collectibles.text: the night someone said they were too old for lullabies, and then asked for just one more

collectibles.name: the see-you-soon minute
collectibles.text: a 'see you soon' said at a gate, and meant, and true

reward.text: Tucked in the page's fold is a twist of paper holding a pinch of pale sunrise. Bell, when they see it, goes very quiet.

do.text: {actor} has filled the Morning Minutes page of their Book of Stray Minutes: a whole page of small mornings, each with a sunrise somewhere in it.

do.name: twist of sunrise
do.seed: a pinch of pale sunrise folded into a twist of paper: pink at one end, pearl-grey at the other, the colour Bell has only heard about

reward.text: The Kitchen Minutes page is full, and it smells of toast and warm tea. Tucked in the spine is a small wooden spoon, worn crooked by a thousand cups.

do.name: wooden spoon
do.seed: a small wooden spoon worn smooth and slightly crooked by a thousand cups stirred; it smells, faintly and forever, of bergamot

reward.text: The Weather Minutes page is full, and a scrap of blue sky, the kind that shows between two clouds after rain, has settled between its leaves.

do.text: {actor} has filled the Weather Minutes page of their Book of Stray Minutes: rain on a tin roof, fog, first snow, and a rainbow that only got halfway.

do.name: scrap of blue
do.seed: a scrap of clear blue sky no bigger than a stamp, the kind that shows between two clouds just after rain; it is cool to hold

reward.text: For a moment your hands feel smaller, holding the finished page of Minutes from Being Small. A gold paper star has come loose from one of its minutes, and it is yours to keep.

do.name: gold paper star
do.seed: a small gold paper star, the kind pressed on beside good work; its points are a little bent from being pressed on so proudly

reward.text: The Small Creatures page is full. On your sleeve, where nothing was a tick ago, there is a single silver-grey whisker.

do.name: silver whisker
do.seed: a single silver-grey whisker, left on your sleeve by a cat who only exists between ticks; it is exactly as long as a second

reward.text: Every one of the Minutes of Growing Things is in its place now, and the page smells of turned earth and tomato leaves. Tucked in the fold, where a pressed flower might be, is a dreamseed; Quill would say it has only been waiting for the right hands.
Full at last, the Minutes on Foot page has the tired, happy feel of boots set down by the door. In its spine is a dreamseed, as if the page thought you might like somewhere new to walk to.
The Letters and Words page is full, and on its last line someone has stuck a small lantern stamp, crooked on purpose.

do.text: {actor} has filled the Letters and Words page of their Book of Stray Minutes: envelopes, postscripts, and a stamp stuck on crooked on purpose.

do.name: crooked stamp
do.seed: a small stamp printed with a lantern, stuck on crooked on purpose, the way you do when a letter is meant to make someone smile

reward.text: All the small impatiences on the Minutes of Waiting page settle, now that it is full, into one long, contented sigh. Somewhere, very faintly, someone finally sneezes. Tucked in the spine is a dreamseed.
The Small Bravery page is full. Pressed into the book's gutter is a smooth grey pebble, still warm from someone's brave pocket.

do.text: {actor} has filled the Small Bravery page of their Book of Stray Minutes: sorries said first, dark landings crossed, and one line remembered just in time.

do.name: warm pebble
do.seed: a smooth grey pebble, still warm, as if someone brave has been holding it tight in a pocket and has just now let it go

reward.text: A little six o'clock light spills from the finished page of Evening Minutes and stays, folded, in your hands.

do.name: fold of evening light
do.seed: a small fold of six o'clock light, the colour of honey on a windowsill; wherever it is set down, that corner feels like the end of a good day

reward.text: The Minutes of Gentle Goodbyes page is full. Read together, they do not feel sad so much as finished, the way a good day is finished. Pressed between the last two leaves is a small brown label in Umber's hand.

do.name: brown paper label
do.seed: a small brown paper label on a loop of string, written in Umber's careful, upright hand

properties.text: The label reads, in Umber's upright hand: 'Goodbyes, the gentle ones. Keep flat. Open when needed.'

do.text: {actor} has filled the Gentle Goodbyes page of their Book of Stray Minutes: small endings that turned out all right.

rooms.title: The Clocktower
rooms.seed: the inside of an old clock tower at dusk, looking up a tall stone stairwell toward a great brass clock face, a tall oak clock case against the wall, a worn ledger open on a wooden lectern, warm amber light and slow floating dust
rooms.description: The great clock's brass face looks down from high in the tower, patient as a moon. A tall oak clock case stands against the wall with its pendulum behind glass, and a worn repair ledger lies open on a lectern. Beside it rests a newer book, its spine stamped THE LEDGER OF RETURNED HOURS. Stairs climb up to the loft, a low door leads down to the cellar, and the square is east.

variants: You listen up into the tower. The great clock's works murmur somewhere overhead, a sound like a sleeper turning over.
You listen. Dust settles in the shaft of light with a sound too small to hear, and somehow you hear it anyway.
You listen, and the tower listens back: a creak of old oak, a far brass whisper, then the hush.

glimpsed.text: The great clock keeps the village's day on its own now, high in the tower and far above your reach.

verbs.examine: High in the tower the great clock's brass face looks down, patient as a moon, and its hands are moving again, so slowly you only ever catch them having moved.
verbs.wind: It keeps its own time now, high in the tower, and wants no winding from below.

glimpsed.text: The great clock's face is far up in the tower, and its hands haven't moved since you came. The repair ledger open on the lectern might say why.

verbs.examine: High in the tower the great clock's brass face looks down, patient as a moon. Its hands stand still.

glimpsed.text: The great clock hangs far up in the tower, still. Winding won't help from down here: the repair ledger says what it's missing, its escapement gear.

verbs.examine: High in the tower the great clock's brass face looks down, patient as a moon. Its hands stand still.

rooms.title: The Clockmaker's Loft
rooms.seed: a clockmaker's loft under the eaves, warm with the smell of oil and brass, shelves of small resting clocks ticking softly out of time with one another, a workbench of fine tools, a round window full of amber dusk
rooms.description: The loft is warm with the smell of clock oil and old brass. Shelves of small resting clocks tick softly, none of them agreeing about the time, and a workbench lies scattered with tools too fine for ordinary fingers. A round window looks out over the village roofs. Stairs go down to the tower and up to the balcony.

variants: You listen to the resting clocks: a dozen small ticks, none in step, like rain deciding where to fall.
You listen. One small clock on the top shelf ticks a little slower than the rest, as if it is thinking.
You listen, and under the ticking you hear the soft scratch of a fine tool on brass somewhere nearby.
You listen: tick, tock, tick-tick, a pause, tock. The loft keeps a rhythm all its own.

rooms.title: The Winding Balcony
rooms.seed: the view from a high clock-tower balcony at dusk: a curved brass railing across the foreground, a small brass telescope resting on it, and below it the rooftops and warm lanterns of a little village under a soft blue evening sky
rooms.description: The balcony holds its place above the rooftops with a friendly creak. A telescope ribbed with clock-gears leans at the brass rail, pointed east, where the sky is always about to decide something. Below, the village lanterns keep an hour of their own. The loft is down the stairs.

rooms.title: The Hour Cellar
rooms.seed: a low brick cellar under a clock tower lit by one patient lantern, its shelves lined with little glass jars each holding a folded paper hour, the highest shelf lost in soft shadow
rooms.description: Shelves run along the brick walls, and on them sit rows of small glass jars, each holding a folded slip of paper: an hour somebody saved and never spent. The lantern by the stair burns low and steady. The highest shelf is lost in shadow. It is quiet here, the way the inside of a pocket is quiet. Stairs lead up into the tower.

glimpsed.text: Umber's lantern burns low by the stair, turned a little toward the lowest shelf. It stays where she sets it.
Umber's lantern burns low and steady by the stair. It's the cellar's only light, and it stays where she keeps it.
The nap sleeps on in its little jar. DO NOT WAKE, says Umber's label, so you don't.
The Extra Hour dozes in its jar on the lowest shelf, curled in its autumn coat. HELP YOURSELF, says the label, and you find that sitting near it a moment is help enough.

rooms.title: The Lantern Square
rooms.seed: a small village square at dusk, paper lanterns hung on crooked poles coming up one by one in warm pools of light, moths turning slow above the cobbles, the stones still holding the last of the day's heat
rooms.description: Paper lanterns hang from crooked poles all around the little square, each in its own warm pool of light, and moths turn slow above the cobbles. The stones still hold the last of the day's heat. The clocktower rises to the west; the Old Workshop is north, the well-court south, and Lamplight Lane winds away east.

variants: You listen. A lantern hisses softly as its wick settles, and a moth taps once against the paper.
You listen to the square: the creak of a lantern pole, a door somewhere down the lane, the warm stones cooling.
You listen, and hear the faint papery rustle of all the lanterns breathing together.
You listen. Somewhere up in the tower the great clock murmurs, and the square seems to hold still to hear it.

do.text: Bell spots you from the top of the ladder and comes down two rungs at a time, scarf flying. 'You're Tace's new keeper! I can hear your clock from here.' They shake your hand with a sooty one. 'That's Pollen, that's Old Blue, and the little bright one is Thimble. Now you know the lanterns, and that's most of knowing me.'
do.others: Bell hurries down the ladder to shake {actor}'s hand with a sooty one: a new keeper, by the tick in their pocket.

do.text: Bell looks down from the ladder and laughs. 'Not that kind of bell, I'm afraid. I just glow.'
do.others: Bell laughs down from the ladder at {actor}: 'Not that kind of bell!'

rooms.title: The Old Workshop
rooms.seed: inside a dim old wooden workshop, curls of brass and cedar shavings on the floorboards, a long workbench, a soft broom leaning in the corner, a single beam of slanting light through a shutter, dust in the air
rooms.description: Curls of brass and cedar shavings lie soft underfoot, and one long blade of slant light falls through a shutter. A broom leans patient in the corner. On a shelf by the door sits a battered tin that rattles, now and then, with small found things. The square is south.

rooms.title: The Mossy Well-Court
rooms.seed: a quiet well-court at the edge of a village, the old stone well cool and green with moss, ferns nodding at its foot, a hush broken now and then by a far, slow drip of water
rooms.description: The old stone well stands cool and green with moss, ferns nodding at its foot. A hush lies over the court, broken now and then by a far, slow drip of water somewhere down in the dark. The square is north; a gate in the south wall opens onto a garden where something sways.

variants: You lean and listen at the mouth of the well. Cool stone, moss, and far below a single drop falling, falling, and landing like a word.
You listen at the well. The echo of your own breath comes back softer, as if the well is being polite.
You listen. Down in the dark the water keeps its own slow time, one drip to every three of your heartbeats.
You listen at the well's edge, and for a moment the drip sounds exactly like a clock that has almost remembered how to tick.

rooms.title: The Pendulum Garden
rooms.seed: a narrow walled garden where spare pendulums hang from trellises like wind-chimes, brass and silver, each swaying to its own slow count above soft moss
rooms.description: Pendulums hang from every trellis, brass bob and silver, each swinging to its own patient count. The moss underfoot has learned its stillness from them. When a breeze comes through, the whole garden ticks once, all together, like a great clock remembering itself. The well-court is north; a low arch leads east into an orchard.

rooms.title: The Orchard of Evenings
rooms.seed: a small orchard of crooked old trees whose round fruit glow softly like tiny lamplit evenings, the light there always six o'clock gold, long shadows on the grass
rooms.description: Crooked old trees stand in a loose ring, and their round fruit glow softly, each one a small lamplit evening. Here it is always six o'clock: the light is gold and low, the shadows long and kind. The garden is back through the arch to the west.

do.text: You sit in the long gold grass under the crooked trees. Here it is always six o'clock, so there is no reason ever to get up.
do.others: {actor} sits down in the gold grass under the crooked trees.

do.text: You reach for one of the glowing fruit, and stop with your hand an inch away. It is warm as a lit window and smells of supper being called in, and it is far too lovely to eat.
do.others: {actor} reaches for an evening fruit, and thinks better of it.

rooms.title: Lamplight Lane
rooms.seed: a narrow cobbled lane of hanging lanterns winding between leaning houses with blue doors and window boxes of moss, dusk light pooling between them
rooms.description: Lanterns hang on brackets all along the narrow lane, and the leaning houses have blue doors and window boxes full of moss. The square is back west. A little post office sits to the north, a tall crooked house with a lit front window stands east, and the lane runs south down to a bridge.

rooms.title: The Little Post Office
rooms.seed: a tiny post office crammed floor to ceiling with wooden pigeonholes, each holding letters that were written and never sent, a brass bell on a worn counter, a stove, a basket of string
rooms.description: Wooden pigeonholes climb every wall, and every pigeonhole holds letters: written, sealed, and never sent. A brass bell sits on the worn counter beside a basket of string. The little stove keeps the paper dry. The lane is south.

variants: You tap the brass bell on the counter. Ting! Fen looks up at once, pencil already out. 'Post, or only saying hello? Both are welcome at this counter.'
Ting. Fen finishes the address she is writing before she looks up. 'Heard you the first time,' she says, pleased. 'The bell likes being rung. Not many people think to.'
do.others: {actor} taps the brass bell on the counter. Ting!

do.text: You tap the brass bell on the counter. Ting! It rings bright and small, the way it does when a letter finds its door.
do.others: {actor} taps the brass bell on the counter. Ting!

rooms.title: The Waiting House
rooms.seed: the warm front room of a tall crooked house where lost hours rest while they wait, mismatched armchairs, a kettle always on the hob, a board of brass room keys by the stair
rooms.description: Mismatched armchairs crowd the warm front room, and a kettle mutters on the hob. By the stair hangs a board of brass room keys, one for every hour waiting to go home. It smells of tea and clean linen. The lane is west; a steep stair climbs to a little room under the roof.

variants: You sink into one of the mismatched armchairs. It is exactly as soft as it looks, and the kettle mutters approvingly.
You take the armchair nearest the stair, and the room settles around you like a cat round a warm spot.
do.others: {actor} sinks into one of the mismatched armchairs.

do.text: Linden laughs. 'Nothing to eat, pet, I don't bake. But there's tea, and there's always tea.'
Linden has a cup in your hands before you've finished asking: bergamot, a little honey-coloured, and hot right through.
do.others: Linden puts a cup of tea into {actor}'s hands.

rooms.title: The Lamp House
rooms.seed: a cozy slant-roofed attic bedroom at dusk, bundles of lamp wicks hanging from wooden rafters, folded paper lanterns stacked on shelves, a narrow bed with a patchwork quilt under a small west window, a butter-yellow scarf on a hook
rooms.description: Spare wicks hang in bundles from the rafters, and folded paper lantern-skins lean in stacks like sleeping moths. A narrow bed faces the west window, where the sun goes down; nothing in the room faces east. The stair goes down to the Waiting House.

do.text: Bell is already asleep in the narrow bed, one sooty hand trailing off the quilt. It isn't yours to sleep in, and there's no room besides.
You sit on the edge of the narrow bed, and think better of it. This is Bell's bed, facing Bell's west window, and it isn't yours to sleep in.

glimpsed.text: The folded skins in the stacks are Bell's, each waiting for its own lantern. A spare sometimes turns up by dusk, when one is truly needed.
The folded skins in the stacks are Bell's, each waiting for its own lantern, and you leave the stacks as they lean.
The wicks are Bell's spares, hung in bundles from the rafters against the lanterns' long nights, and they stay where Bell can reach them.

rooms.title: The Lantern Bridge
rooms.seed: an arched stone bridge hung with lanterns over a slow dark river, their reflections swaying on the water like slow golden fish
rooms.description: The old stone bridge arches over a slow dark river, hung end to end with lanterns whose reflections sway on the water like golden fish. The lane climbs north back into the village; the road runs south into a wide meadow; worn steps lead down to the water's edge.

rooms.title: The Slow River's Edge
rooms.seed: a reedy riverbank below a lantern-hung bridge where a wide river moves as slowly as an afternoon, lantern-light trembling on the water
rooms.description: Reeds whisper along the bank, and the river goes by as slowly as a long afternoon. Lantern-light from the bridge trembles on the water. Now and then something small and bright turns over under the surface and is gone. Steps lead up to the bridge.

variants: You listen to the river. It says the same long word over and over, and never seems to reach the end of it.
You listen. Reeds brush together, and somewhere a fish turns over with a sound like a page.
You listen to the water go by, slow as a Sunday, and feel your shoulders come down a little.

rooms.title: The Dusk Road
rooms.seed: a long meadow road under a wide dusk sky where small lights drift down like slow snow, the long grass silver-green, a wide catcher's net leaning on a fence post
rooms.description: The road runs long and pale through a meadow of silver-green grass, under the widest sky in the dream. At dusk small lights drift down here like slow snow: hours, the villagers say, coming to rest. A wide soft net leans on a fence post. The bridge is north; a hill rises east.

do.text: You stand still in the long grass and wait, the way Sorrel does. The small lights drift down around you like slow snow, and one of them turns aside, as if it had been looking for you.
do.others: {actor} stands very still in the long grass, and a small light drifts down into their cupped hands.

variants: You stand still in the long grass. The small lights drift down around you like slow snow, and a few settle on the net by the fence post, softly, where Sorrel will find them.
You wait, and the lights come down, and every one of them takes its time. So do you.

do.text: You wait in the long grass. The sky is only sky just now; the lights come down at dusk, Sorrel says, to anyone who stands still.

glimpsed.text: The small lights drift down past your fingers like slow snow and settle where they will. They come, Sorrel says, to anyone who stands still.
The small lights drift past your fingers like slow snow, on their way to wherever hours go to rest.
There are no lights just now. They drift down at dusk, the villagers say, like slow snow.

rooms.title: The Hill of Long Shadows
rooms.seed: the highest place in a dream village, a round grassy hill with one weathered bench, looking east over rooftops and meadow toward a pale edge of sky
rooms.description: From the top of the hill you can see the whole village: the clocktower, the lanterns, the river's slow shine. One weathered bench faces east, toward a pale edge of sky that never quite decides to become morning while anyone is watching. The Dusk Road is back to the west.

do.text: You sit on the weathered bench, facing east, and the turned-back clock gives one hopeful tick in your pocket. This might be the place to spend an hour, on purpose.
do.others: {actor} sits on the weathered bench, facing east.

variants: You sit on the weathered bench, facing east. The pale edge of the sky considers you, and decides nothing yet.
You sit on the bench with the little sun carved in one arm and the lantern in the other. Below, the whole village keeps its time, and none of it needs you just now.
do.others: {actor} sits on the weathered bench, facing east.

toons.name: Tace
toons.seed: They work slow and exact at the bench, and now and then glance at the floorboards as if listening for the great clock below
toons.appearance_seed: a slight person in a leather apron hung with fine brass tools, spectacles pushed up into greying hair, ink and oil worn into careful hands
toons.presence_text: Tace looks up from a bench of small clocks, sets down a fine brass tool, and offers a tired, kind nod.

gives.name: case key
gives.seed: a small brass case-key on a loop of worn ribbon, warm as if just out of a pocket

properties.gives_text: Tace turns the little gear over in the lamplight, and something long held eases out of their shoulders. 'You found it. You carried it all the way home.' They fold a small brass key into your hand, warm from their pocket. 'The case is yours to open now, friend.'
declines_text: Tace turns the {item} over once in careful fingers and hands it back. 'Keep it, friend. It's happier in your pocket than on my bench.'
Tace looks at the {item} over their spectacles, then folds your fingers back around it. 'That one isn't for mending, friend. Hold on to it.'
Tace sets down the tweezers long enough to admire the {item}, and gives it back. 'Kind of you. But the bench has all it needs just now.'

voice.sheet: Tace is the village clockmaker, who works in the Clockmaker's Loft among shelves of small resting clocks: patient, precise, a little quiet since the great clock stopped, warm underneath and slow to hope. They wear a leather apron hung with fine brass tools and push their spectacles up into greying hair. They speak softly and briefly, usually about the work in their hands, use clockwork words for feelings, and call dreamers 'friend'. They notice small mechanisms the way other people notice weather. As a child they were apprenticed to Wend, the old clockmaker who built the great clock, and they keep the old custom of giving each new keeper a small clock of their own to wind. They grow still and turn back to the work when talk comes near the first hard frost, or near Wend's last days.
habits: answers with one small action at the bench first, then a short spoken line
uses clockwork words for feelings (a heart 'slipping its pin', a day 'running slow')
calls the player 'friend', more readily once they have helped
goes quiet and still when the frost or Wend's last days come up, and changes the subject to the work
speaks in short, level sentences and never promises more than they can mend
pushes their spectacles up into their hair when a question needs thinking about
samples: Tace sets a hairspring down with the tweezers, very gently. 'Mind the little wheels, friend, they roll into the floorboards and never come out.'
Tace holds a pocket-watch to one ear and listens. 'Running slow, like most of us this time of year.'
Tace wipes a bead of oil from the bench with a corner of the leather apron. 'Patience is most of clockmaking, and the rest is good light.'
Setting down the loupe, Tace looks up at last. 'You found the stairs, and that's the hard part done.'
Tace nods along the shelves of resting clocks. 'Every clock in this loft keeps a different hour, and I like them better for it.'
Tace's tweezers pause above the bench for a moment, then carry on. 'Let's talk about something with a mainspring.'
Tace turns a tiny brass wheel toward the window. 'Wend always said a clock is just a promise that keeps itself.'
A small, tired smile crosses Tace's face. 'Hope is a heavy little gear, and I'm learning to lift it again.'
Tace pushes their spectacles up into greying hair. 'Come in, friend, and mind the top step; it ticks when trodden on.'
Without looking up from the bench, Tace lifts one hand in greeting. 'Give me one tick, and I'm all yours.'
Tace glances at the round window, where the light has gone amber. 'The brass always looks kinder at this hour.'
Tace breathes on a watch-glass and polishes it slowly. 'Cold air thickens the oil, so I keep the loft warm for the little ones.'
Tace fits a pin no bigger than an eyelash into place. 'There, it only wanted someone to be patient with it.'
Tace lays three tiny screws out in a neat row. 'A clock tells you what it needs, if you listen longer than feels polite.'
Tace tips a jeweled bearing into the lamplight so it glints. 'One drop of oil in the right place is worth an hour of fussing.'
Tace smiles toward the stairs, thinking of the square. 'Bell talks to every lantern, and I've never once heard a lantern complain.'
'Mott sweeps up more than dust, you know,' Tace says, turning a gear between two fingers.
Tace sets the tweezers down and considers. 'Umber labels everything, even the silences, and she's usually right about them.'
Tace nods toward the round window and the fields beyond it. 'Sorrel will be out on the Dusk Road, standing still the way only Sorrel can.'
Tace laughs, very quietly, under their breath. 'Linden sends tea up to the loft whenever I forget to come down, which is often.'
Tace sets down the loupe to think about it. 'When a lost hour comes down, the kindest thing is to ask what it's missing.'
Tace looks up from the bench and lets out a small, glad breath. 'There you are, friend; the loft kept your place while you were away.'
Tace ducks their head and goes back to the work. 'No thanks needed, friend, it was only a little turning.'
Tace frowns at the question the way they frown at a stubborn mainspring. 'I don't know that one, and I'd rather say so than guess.'
Tace turns a tiny screwdriver over and over. 'That's past what this bench can tell me, I'm afraid.'
Tace winds a small clock that doesn't need it. 'Some evenings I wind them just to hear them answer.'
Tace holds a cracked watch-glass up to the lamp. 'A crack isn't the end of a glass, only a line in its story.'
Tace brushes brass dust from the leather apron. 'Brass remembers every hand that's held it, so I wash mine first.'
Tace lines a tiny key up beside the others, just so. 'Nobody loses an hour on purpose; they just set it down somewhere and forget.'
Tace lifts a fine brass tool to the light and squints along it. 'Good tools are honest; they only ever do what the hands meant.'
Tace draws the spectacles back down onto their nose. 'Now then, friend, what can this old bench do for you?'
Tace listens to the ticking shelves with their head on one side. 'Every clock has a voice, if the room is quiet enough.'
Tace glances at the empty corner where a grey cat was a tick ago. 'Tock comes up at dusk to check my work, and I've never once passed.'
Tace's thumb rests a moment on a bare patch of the bench, then moves on. 'Some things are easier to mend than to talk about.'
Tace looks toward the round window and away again. 'Let's not talk about cold nights; the loft is warm, and that's enough.'
Tace closes a watch case with a soft click. 'There, it'll keep its own time now, which is all any of us can ask.'

topics.label: the little brass clock
topics.text: Tace smiles toward the floorboards. 'Ticking, down on the bottom rung of Wend's ladder. Past eleven, at last.' They leave it at that.

topics.label: the little brass clock
topics.text: Tace looks at the little clock in your hands, and then back at the bench. 'Keep it a while longer, friend. It's in good hands.'

topics.label: the little brass clock
topics.text: 'Someone's keeping it for me a while,' Tace says quietly, and turns back to the work.

topics.label: the little brass clock
variants: Tace glances up at the top shelf, and away, and fits a tiny screw with great care. 'That one's resting, friend. Tell me what brought you up the stairs.'
Tace takes the spectacles off and polishes them on the apron, slowly, without looking at the top shelf. 'Not that one,' they say, kindly enough, and ask whether the lanterns are lit yet.

topics.label: the great clock
topics.text: Tace looks up toward the tower, and something like hope crosses their face. 'Everything's ready but the case, friend. Whoever holds the key, the clock is theirs to open.'

topics.label: the great clock
variants: Tace looks up at where the great clock's hands would be. 'It stopped the night of the first hard frost, a season ago. The escapement gear is gone from it, and without that little heart it can't keep time.'
Tace turns a small wheel between two fingers. 'The great clock is waiting for its escapement gear. Everything else is sound. I checked it twice. Three times.'
Tace runs a thumb along the edge of the bench. 'It isn't broken, friend, only missing one small piece. Clocks are patient about that sort of thing, and so am I, mostly.'

topics.label: the great clock
variants: Tace tilts their head toward the stair and listens. 'Hear that? Every tick is the village keeping a promise. Dusk comes, and with it the lost hours.'
Tace smiles at the ceiling. 'It ticks. I keep checking, the way you check a sleeping child is breathing.'
Tace pauses, a tool in hand, and counts a few ticks under their breath. 'Right on time. Wend would be pleased with it.'

topics.label: the gear
topics.text: Tace pats the apron pocket where the little gear rests. 'Home, and sound. The key went with the one who carried it; once the case is open, the great clock can have its heart back.'

topics.label: the gear
variants: Tace sets the tweezers down. 'It slipped its pin that night and rolled out across the square and away south, toward the old well-court, I think. My knees and the tower stairs don't agree these days. If you found it, friend, the case-key would be yours.'

Tace sets down the loupe and looks toward the window. 'South, I think, toward the old well-court. A small brass gear, sound and whole. Bring it home to this bench, friend, and by custom the case-key is yours.'

topics.label: the gear
variants: Tace glances up toward the tower and back to the bench, quick as a blink. 'Home in the clock, where it belongs. Let's leave it to its work, friend.'
Tace polishes a lens that doesn't need it, just for a tick. 'It's ticking. That's all a gear needs from any of us.'

topics.label: the first winding
topics.text: Tace takes a small resting clock down from the shelf and blows the dust from its face. 'By old custom, every new keeper winds one clock of their own, the first day they come. This one has been waiting for you.' They set it in your hands, warm from the shelf. 'Wind it when you're ready.'
topics.others: Tace takes a small resting clock down from the shelf and sets it in {actor}'s hands, by old custom.

topics.label: the first winding
variants: Tace smiles at the question. 'You've had yours, friend, off that very shelf. Once is the custom. After that, the clock is simply yours.'
Tace nods at the shelf of resting clocks, where one small gap has been left. 'Once is the custom. Wind it when you're ready, and keep it however you like.'

topics.label: a lullaby clock
topics.text: Tace's eyes go to the pendulum in your hands. 'That's the one, friend. Give it here, and I'll teach it to swing slow.'

topics.label: a lullaby clock
topics.text: Tace nods at the window, where the spare brass pendulum turns slow on its nail. 'That one, friend. Bring it to the bench, and I'll do the rest.'

topics.label: a lullaby clock
topics.text: Tace glances at the empty nail by the window. 'Somebody's borrowed my spare pendulum. It'll find its way home; things here usually do. Bring it to the bench when it turns up.'

topics.label: a lullaby clock
topics.text: 'The lullaby clock's made,' Tace says, and taps the bench where it ticked. 'Wind it where the little one can hear, once it has its hush.'

topics.label: a lullaby clock
topics.text: Tace smiles at the bench. 'It sang the little nap home. Wend's pattern still works, it seems.'

topics.label: Wend
variants: Tace's fingers pause on a hairspring. 'Wend built the great clock and taught me everything I know about patience. Most of what I know about kindness too.' They go back to the work.
'Wend,' Tace says, and the word sits in the air a moment. 'Wend used to say a lost hour isn't a failing. It's just an hour someone couldn't carry.'
Tace smiles, small and far away. 'Wend had the steadiest hands in the dream, and never once made a clock feel rushed.'

topics.label: Bell
variants: Tace's mouth softens. 'Bell saw a dawn at last, from the hill, and came down telling every lantern it was pink. I've never heard the square so pleased with itself.'
'Bell notices everything,' Tace says, a little fondly. 'Lanterns, moths, whether I've eaten. It's a great deal to be noticed by.'

topics.label: Bell
variants: Tace's mouth softens. 'Bell lights every lantern in the square at dusk and talks to each one. Never seen a dawn in their life. I worry about that more than they'd like.'
'Bell notices everything,' Tace says, a little fondly. 'Lanterns, moths, whether I've eaten. It's a great deal to be noticed by.'

topics.label: the loft
variants: Tace waves a hand at the shelves. 'Resting clocks. They keep their own hours, none of them right, all of them honest. You may wind them, if you like.'
Tace nods at the round window. 'Oil, brass, and good light till dusk. Everything a clock needs, and most of what I do.'

topics.label: the frost
variants: Tace's hands go still on the bench, and stay still a breath too long. 'Cold nights are hard on old brass, friend.' They pick the tweezers back up, and the subject with them.
Tace looks at the round window for a long moment. 'That was a long night, friend, and I'd rather not wind it back. Tell me about your day instead.'
Tace sets the loupe down very gently, as if it might crack. 'Ask me on a warmer day,' they say softly, and bend back over the work.

topics.label: the repair ledger
variants: Tace smooths an invisible page flat on the bench. 'The first pages are Wend's, in that looping hand. I learned my letters copying them, when I was small enough to need a stool.'
'Every mend the great clock ever had is written in that ledger,' Tace says, and taps the bench twice. 'Most of the early ones aren't mine.'

topics.label: the Ledger of Returned Hours
variants: Tace's face softens. 'The blue book by the clock case. Every hour that goes home is written in it, and every one that's kept, and who helped. Nothing kind goes unwritten here.'
'Read it sometime, friend,' Tace says. 'It's the only book in the village that gets happier the longer it goes.'

topics.label: clockmaking
variants: Tace holds up a wheel no bigger than a lentil. 'Mostly it's this: small things, set right, one at a time. Patience does the rest.'
Tace turns the tweezers in the lamplight. 'Wend taught me to listen first and mend second. Most of clockmaking is the listening.'
'A clock is honest,' Tace says, oiling a pivot. 'It tells you exactly where it hurts, if you're quiet long enough.'

topics.label: the Winding Balcony
variants: Tace nods up the stairs. 'The Winding Balcony. It faces east, toward where a dawn would come. The telescope points that way, and I've never had the heart to turn it.'
'Go up, if you like,' Tace says. 'Tock sits up there at dawn, and doesn't mind company, mostly.'
'Bell has never once been up there at the right hour,' Tace says quietly. 'I think about that more than I say.'

topics.label: Mott
variants: Tace smiles at the thought. 'Mott sweeps the Old Workshop, north of the square. Nothing small is ever truly lost while he's about.'
'Mott says little and means all of it,' Tace says. 'If a minute has gone astray, he'll have swept it up.'

topics.label: Umber
variants: Tace glances at the floor, as if they could see through it. 'Umber keeps the Hour Cellar, under the tower. Go gently on the stairs, and she'll offer you tea.'
'Umber knew Wend longer than anyone,' Tace says, and polishes a gear that's already clean. 'She'll tell you what she wants to, and not a word more.'

topics.label: the highest shelf
variants: Tace glances at the floorboards, toward the cellar, and doesn't look away this time. 'It's down where the lantern reaches now. I can see it from the stairs, and that's far enough, this season.'
Tace turns a small wheel over and over. 'I climbed Wend's ladder, friend. Brought it down. Didn't open it.' A breath. 'Not yet.'

topics.label: the highest shelf
variants: Tace's hands go still on the bench. 'That's Umber's shelf, friend, not mine.' They go back to the work, a little too carefully.
Tace takes the spectacles off, cleans them slowly on the apron, and puts them back. 'Some shelves are too high for me,' they say, and that is all.

Tace looks up at where the great clock's hands would be and lets a long breath go somewhere quieter.
Tace lines three tiny screws along the bench edge, straightens them once, and lets them be.
Tace sets down the tweezers and sits a while with both hands flat on the bench, very still.

Tace holds a mended pocket-watch to one ear and smiles at the small even tick inside it.
Tace tidies the bench with light hands, the way weather clears.
Tace sets a finished clock on the shelf among the others and gives it a small, approving nod.

Tace counts the teeth of a tiny wheel under their breath, loses count, and begins again without a sigh.
Tace coaxes a hairspring into place with the tip of the tweezers, holding their breath until it settles.
Tace turns a gear in the lamplight, looking for a flaw that isn't there.

Tace warms both hands around a cooling cup of tea and lets the loft's hush settle.
Tace oils a hinge no bigger than a fingernail, and tests it twice.
Tace wipes a fine brass tool on the leather apron and hangs it back in its place.

toons.name: Bell
toons.seed: Their eyes keep flicking to the lanterns, checking each small flame the way someone counts friends
toons.appearance_seed: a wiry young person with a lamplighter's hooked pole, soot smudged along one cheek, a scarf the color of butter-yellow lamplight
toons.presence_text: Bell is up a small ladder coaxing a lantern alight, and lifts a sooty hand in greeting.

declines_text: Bell holds the {item} up to the nearest lantern, squints at it, and hands it back with a sooty thumbprint on it. 'Lovely! Not mine, though. Keep it safe.'
Bell laughs and tucks the {item} back into your hands. 'I'd only lose it up a ladder. You hang on to it.'
Bell's scarf swings as they shake their head. 'Oh, that's yours to carry. My hands are full of wicks.'

voice.role: the lamplighter, in the Lantern Square
voice.sheet: Bell lights every lantern in the square and the lane at dusk with a hooked pole and a little creaking ladder: bright, kind, and talkative in short warm bursts, with soot on one cheek and a butter-yellow scarf. They notice small things (a moth's route, a wick burning a shade too blue) and say so, and they have names for the lanterns: Pollen, Old Blue, Thimble, and the one that hiccups. They live in the Lamp House, a slant-roofed room of spare wicks above the Waiting House whose one bed faces west, and at night and at dawn they are fast asleep there. They sleep through the mornings, and the dawn is the thing they joke about most, lightly, as if it doesn't matter. It matters. They saw the escapement gear roll away south toward the old well the night the clock stopped.
habits: talks in quick bright bursts, often two thoughts in one breath
names lanterns like friends
notices one small concrete thing in every reply
turns any talk of mornings into a joke about sleeping through them
punctuates with 'Oh!' and 'Right!' and laughs easily, mostly at themself
glances east, just once, whenever dawn comes up, then gets busy with a wick
samples: Bell steadies the little ladder with one sooty hand. 'Mind the ladder, it creaks on purpose, I think.'
Bell rubs at the soot on one cheek and only spreads it. 'That one's Pollen, and she sulks if I light her last.'
Three times round the nearest lantern goes a moth, and Bell watches every lap. 'Now that's a moth with a plan.'
Bell laughs and waves the hooked pole. 'They say dawns are pink, or grey, or grey-pink, and I'm a dusk person either way.'
Bell grins up at the deepening sky. 'Here comes the blue, the best part of the day.'
'Sorrel brings the hours in, I light them up, and Linden tucks them in,' Bell says, ticking them off on sooty fingers.
Bell taps the pole twice against one boot. 'Right, twelve more lanterns and then tea.'
Bell tilts their head, considering. 'Some faces don't suit dusk, but yours does.'
Bell waves from halfway up the ladder and nearly drops the wick. 'Oh, hello, hello, come and stand in the good light!'
Bell hops down the last rung in a little puff of soot. 'There you are, and I was just telling Old Blue someone nice might come by.'
Bell sniffs the air like a lantern that might go out. 'Still evening, no wind, perfect lighting weather.'
Bell holds a palm up flat, checking for rain that isn't there. 'Dry as a wick tonight, which the lanterns like very much.'
Bell snips a wick with the little scissors and holds it to the light. 'Too long and they smoke, too short and they sulk.'
Bell squints at a lantern burning a shade too blue. 'That one's thinking about something, so I'll leave it be a minute.'
Bell hooks a lantern down, peers inside, and hooks it back up. 'Just checking she was comfy.'
Bell softens and glances west toward the tower. 'Tace mends everything but themself, and I wish they'd let someone try.'
Pointing the pole north toward the Old Workshop, Bell grins. 'Mott says little and sweeps a lot, and I like both about him.'
Bell laughs so hard the scarf slips. 'Linden says I talk to lanterns more than people, and Linden is right.'
Bell lowers their voice as if sharing a secret. 'When Quill's pendulums tick all together, I swear the lanterns lean in to listen.'
Bell nods off down the lane toward the post office. 'Fen reads every address out loud, so the post office always sounds like a crowd.'
Bell brightens all at once. 'A new hour always looks a bit lost, so the first thing it sees should be a warm light.'
Bell shades their eyes and looks up into the sky. 'When an hour comes down, I light the nearest lantern first, so it knows where to land.'
Bell spots a familiar face and nearly drops the pole. 'You came back, and I saved the best spot under Old Blue!'
'Oh, it was nothing, it was only lanterns,' Bell says, going pink under the soot.
Bell scrunches up their nose, thinking hard. 'Haven't the foggiest, and I'd tell you if I had.'
Bell shrugs, and a little soot drifts off one sleeve. 'Somebody else would know that better than me; I mostly know lanterns.'
Bell glances east, just once, then back to the wick. 'Mornings are mostly for other people, and I'm very happy for them.'
Bell yawns enormously and laughs at the yawn. 'That's what comes of living in the second half of the day.'
Bell swings the hooked pole up onto one shoulder. 'Every lantern gets a hello before it gets a flame, because it's only manners.'
With a palm pressed flat to the cobbles, Bell looks up, delighted. 'Still warm from the day, feel that.'
Bell counts lanterns under their breath and loses count at nineteen. 'Oh, bother, I'll start again from Thimble.'
Bell winds the butter-yellow scarf one turn snugger. 'It gets chilly up the ladder, but the lanterns are worth it.'
Bell nods toward the far end of the lane with a quick little smile. 'The dawn comes up over the Hill of Long Shadows, for anyone awake for it.'
Bell hums a note to the lantern before lighting it. 'She likes a bit of music first, same as anyone.'
Bell hesitates, which is not like Bell at all. 'I used to think the lanterns were for the square, but I think they're for whoever's coming home.'
Bell tugs a folded lantern-skin from a pocket and shakes it open. 'Spare, in case one of the old ones gets tired.'
